questions.question_text: Across which axis does the graph of $y=f(-x)$ reflect the graph of $y=f(x)$?

options.why: A minus inside $f$ changes $x$, not $y$, so it flips across the $y$-axis.
Only one minus is present, so only one axis is involved.
Replacing $x$ with $-x$ is a reflection, not a slide.

questions.solution_text:
The minus is inside $f$: $(x,y)\to(-x,y)$.
Reflection across the $y$-axis.

questions.question_text:
The point $(7,3)$ lies on $y=f(x)$.
What is its image on the graph of $y=-f(x)$?

options.why: A minus outside $f$ changes $y$, not $x$; that image is for $f(-x)$.
Only the $y$-coordinate changes sign for $-f(x)$, not both.
Reflection does not swap the coordinates.

questions.question_text: Given $f(x)=x^{2}-6x$, which is the equation of $y=-f(x)$?

options.why: Only the first term was negated; the whole rule must change sign.
Only the second term was negated; every term must change sign.
This is $f(x)$ unchanged; a minus outside negates the whole rule.
Then the $x$-coordinate would change sign, but here $x=1$ stayed.
Then both coordinates would change sign, but here $x$ stayed the same.
The curve was flipped across the $x$-axis, not slid upward.

questions.solution_text:
Only the $y$-coordinate changed sign: $(x,y)\to(x,-y)$.
Reflection across the $x$-axis, $y=-f(x)$.

questions.question_text:
The point $(-6,5)$ lies on $y=f(x)$.
What is its image on the graph of $y=-f(-x)$?

options.why: For $-f(-x)$ the $x$-coordinate must also change sign, not stay $-6$.
The $y$-coordinate must also change sign for $-f(-x)$.
This is the original point; both coordinates change sign under $-f(-x)$.

questions.question_text: For which function is the graph of $y=f(-x)$ identical to the graph of $y=f(x)$?

options.why: Here $f(-x)=-x^{3}=-f(x)$, an odd function, so the $y$-axis image differs.
Here $f(-x)=2^{-x}\neq f(x)$, so the $y$-axis reflection changes it.
Here $f(-x)=\sqrt{-x}$ has a different domain, so it is not identical.

questions.solution_text:
$f(-x)=(-x)^{2}=x^{2}=f(x)$
An even function is unchanged by a $y$-axis reflection.

options.why: A $y$-axis reflection leaves this symmetric parabola looking unchanged.
Both-axis reflection here would also match the original parabola shape wrongly; only $y$ changed sign.
The curve was flipped to open downward, not slid down.

questions.solution_text:
Each point $(x,y)$ became $(x,-y)$: the curve opens the opposite way.
Reflection across the $x$-axis.
